articles.title: Name and territory of the Union
articles.s: Declares India a Union of States and defines its territory: the states, the Union Territories in the First Schedule, and any territories that may be acquired. Exam point: India is a Union, not the result of an agreement among states, so no state has a right to secede.

articles.title: Admission or establishment of new States
articles.s: Gives Parliament the power to admit new states into the Union or establish new states on such terms as it thinks fit (used when Sikkim joined in 1975). Such laws need only a simple majority.

articles.title: Sikkim to be associated with the Union
articles.s: Inserted by the 35th Amendment 1975 giving Sikkim the special status of an associate state; omitted by the 36th Amendment 1975 when Sikkim became a full state of the Union.

articles.title: Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States
articles.s: Lets Parliament form a new state, increase or reduce a state's area, change its boundaries or rename it (used for state reorganisations like Andhra Pradesh/Telangana and the J and K reorganisation). Needs only a simple majority; the affected state legislature is consulted but its view is not binding.

articles.title: Laws made under articles 2 and 3 to provide for the amendment of the First and the Fourth Schedules and supplemental, incidental and consequential matters
articles.s: Laws under Articles 2 and 3 may amend the First and Fourth Schedules and include consequential provisions; such laws are not treated as constitutional amendments under Article 368.

articles.title: Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
articles.s: Every person domiciled in India at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950) who was born in India, or whose parents were born in India, or who had ordinarily lived in India for five years, became a citizen.

articles.title: Rights of citizenship of certain persons who have migrated to India from Pakistan
articles.s: Grants citizenship to persons who migrated to India from Pakistan: those who came before 19 July 1948 became citizens if resident since migration, while later migrants had to register with an appointed officer.

articles.title: Rights of citizenship of certain migrants to Pakistan
articles.s: Denies citizenship at commencement to anyone who migrated from India to Pakistan after 1 March 1947, except a person who returned to India under a permit for resettlement.

articles.title: Rights of citizenship of certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India
articles.s: Gives citizenship rights to a person of Indian origin residing outside India who registered as a citizen with an Indian diplomatic or consular representative.

articles.title: Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State not to be citizens
articles.s: Anyone who voluntarily acquires the citizenship of a foreign state automatically ceases to be an Indian citizen; India does not permit dual citizenship.

articles.title: Continuance of the rights of citizenship
articles.s: Every person who is a citizen under Part II continues to be one, subject to any law made by Parliament.

articles.title: Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law
articles.s: Empowers Parliament to make laws on acquisition and termination of citizenship; this is the constitutional basis of the Citizenship Act, 1955.

articles.title: Definition
articles.s: Defines 'the State' for Fundamental Rights: it includes the Government and Parliament of India, state governments and legislatures, and all local and other authorities (such as statutory bodies and public corporations) within India.
articles.detail: It defines the term "State" for the purpose of Fundamental Rights, covering the government, Parliament, state legislatures, and other authorities.

articles.title: Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights
articles.s: All pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void to the extent of the inconsistency, and the State cannot make laws that take away or abridge FRs. This is the textual basis of judicial review (Golaknath, Kesavananda Bharati).
articles.detail: It declares that any law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights is void, and it is the basis of judicial review in India.

articles.title: Equality before law
articles.s: Guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to all persons. It permits reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the law's object, but forbids arbitrary or discriminatory state action.
articles.detail: It guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to every person in India.

articles.title: Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
articles.s: Bars the State from discriminating against citizens on these grounds, and bars discrimination in access to public places. Clauses (3), (4), (5) and (6) allow special provisions for women, children, SCs, STs, socially and educationally backward classes, and economically weaker sections (EWS reservation).
articles.detail: It prohibits discrimination against any citizen on the grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.

articles.title: Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
articles.s: Guarantees equality of opportunity in state employment and bars discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence. Clauses (4), (4A) and (4B) permit reservation for backward classes, SCs and STs in appointments and promotions, with the 50 percent ceiling from Indra Sawhney (1992).
articles.detail: It guarantees equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters of public employment.

articles.title: Abolition of Untouchability
articles.s: Abolishes untouchability in all forms and makes enforcing any disability arising from it a punishable offence (Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955). It is an absolute right available against private individuals as well.
articles.detail: It abolishes untouchability and makes its practice in any form an offence punishable by law.

articles.title: Abolition of titles
articles.s: Abolishes all titles except military and academic distinctions. Citizens cannot accept titles from foreign states, and foreigners holding offices of profit or trust need the President's consent to accept any foreign title or present.
articles.detail: It abolishes titles, so the state cannot confer titles except military and academic distinctions.

articles.title: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
articles.s: Protects six freedoms: speech and expression, peaceful assembly without arms, forming associations or unions, free movement, residence and settlement, and practising any profession or trade. Each is subject to reasonable restrictions on grounds such as sovereignty, security, public order, decency, morality and contempt of court.
articles.detail: It protects six freedoms: speech and expression, peaceful assembly, association, free movement, residence and settlement, and practising any profession or occupation. These freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions.

articles.title: Protection in respect of conviction for offences
articles.s: Gives three criminal-justice safeguards: no ex post facto punishment (no conviction under a law made after the act), no double jeopardy (no second prosecution and punishment for the same offence), and no self-incrimination (no person accused of an offence can be compelled to be a witness against himself).
articles.detail: It protects persons accused of offences: no punishment under a law made after the act (ex post facto law), no punishment twice for the same offence (double jeopardy), and no person can be forced to be a witness against himself.

articles.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
articles.s: No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. After Maneka Gandhi (1978) this includes due process in substance, and the Court has read in rights to dignity, privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017), clean environment, speedy trial, legal aid and livelihood.
articles.detail: It guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Courts have read many implied rights into it, including the right to privacy and a clean environment.

articles.title: Right to education
articles.s: Makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right for all children aged 6 to 14 (86th Amendment 2002), implemented through the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009.
articles.detail: Added by the 86th Amendment in 2002, it makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children between 6 and 14 years.

articles.title: Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases
articles.s: An arrested person must be told the grounds of arrest, has the right to consult a lawyer, and must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours. Preventive detention is allowed with safeguards: detention beyond three months needs an Advisory Board's opinion, and Parliament must fix the maximum period (seven months under current law).
articles.detail: It provides safeguards to persons who are arrested or detained, including the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest and the right to consult a lawyer.

articles.title: Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
articles.s: Prohibits human trafficking, begar (forced unpaid labour) and other similar forms of forced labour, making violations punishable (Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976). The State may still impose compulsory public service without discrimination.
articles.detail: It prohibits traffic in human beings, begar, and other forms of forced labour.

articles.title: Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc.
articles.s: Bans employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines or other hazardous work; the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016 extended the ban to all occupations for children below 14.
articles.detail: It prohibits the employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines, or other hazardous work.

articles.title: Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
articles.s: Every person may freely profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, health and other Fundamental Rights. The State may regulate secular activities linked to religion, and Sikhs' wearing of kirpans is expressly protected.
articles.detail: It guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practise, and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, and health.

articles.title: Freedom to manage religious affairs
articles.s: Every religious denomination may establish and maintain religious and charitable institutions, manage its own religious affairs, own and acquire property, and administer it according to law.
articles.detail: It gives every religious denomination the right to manage its own religious affairs, own property, and establish institutions.

articles.title: Freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion
articles.s: No person can be compelled to pay taxes whose proceeds are specifically used to promote or maintain any particular religion or religious denomination.
articles.detail: It says no person can be compelled to pay taxes for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion.

articles.title: Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions
articles.s: Bars religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by the State; in state-aided or recognised institutions, no person can be compelled to take part in religious instruction or worship without consent (or a guardian's consent for minors).
articles.detail: It prohibits religious instruction in educational institutions wholly maintained by state funds.

articles.title: Protection of interests of minorities
articles.s: Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture may conserve it, and no citizen can be denied admission to state-maintained or aided educational institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language.
articles.detail: It protects the right of minorities to conserve their distinct language, script, and culture.

articles.title: Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
articles.s: Religious and linguistic minorities may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice, and the State cannot discriminate against them in granting aid (scope clarified in T.M.A. Pai, 2002).
articles.detail: It gives minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

articles.title: Compulsory acquisition of property
articles.s: Guaranteed the right to property as a fundamental right with compensation for acquisition; repealed by the 44th Amendment 1978, which moved property to Article 300A as a constitutional legal right.

articles.title: Saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates, etc.
articles.s: Protects land-reform and estate-acquisition laws (like zamindari abolition) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 (1st Amendment 1951); upheld in Kesavananda Bharati subject to the basic structure doctrine.

articles.title: Validation of certain Acts and Regulations
articles.s: Validates the Acts listed in the Ninth Schedule against Fundamental Rights challenges; after I.R. Coelho (2007), laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 remain open to basic-structure review.

articles.title: Saving of laws giving effect to certain directive principles
articles.s: Protects laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19; the 42nd Amendment's wider version was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980), leaving the original narrow form intact.

articles.title: Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part
articles.s: Gives every person the right to move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights; Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution. The Court may issue the writs of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari.
articles.detail: It gives every person the right to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution. (Article 31, which dealt with the right to property, was repealed by the 44th Amendment in 1978.) Articles 33, 34 and 35: Article 33 lets Parliament restrict Fundamental Rights of armed forces and police personnel. Article 34 allows restrictions during martial law. Article 35 gives Parliament, not state legislatures, the power to make laws giving effect to Fundamental Rights. The Directive Principles are guidelines for the state in making laws. They are not enforceable in courts, but governments are expected to apply them while governing.

articles.title: Power of Parliament to modify the rights conferred by this Part in their application to Forces, etc.
articles.s: Empowers Parliament to restrict Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces, paramilitary forces, police and intelligence agencies to maintain discipline (Army Act, 1950 and similar laws).

articles.title: Restriction on rights conferred by this Part while martial law is in force in any area
articles.s: Lets Parliament indemnify public servants for acts done to maintain order during martial law and validate their sentences; only Parliament, not state legislatures, may make such a law.

articles.title: Legislation to give effect to the provisions of this Part
articles.s: Reserves to Parliament (excluding state legislatures) the power to make laws giving effect to specified Fundamental Rights and to prescribe punishments for acts declared offences under this Part.

articles.title: Definition
articles.s: Defines 'the State' for the Directive Principles with the same meaning as in Article 12.

articles.title: Application of the principles contained in this Part
articles.s: The Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country and the State must apply them while making laws.

articles.title: State to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people
articles.s: Directs the State to secure a social order with justice (social, economic and political) informing all institutions, and to minimise inequalities of income, status, facilities and opportunities (second clause added by the 44th Amendment 1978).
articles.detail: It directs the state to secure a social order that promotes the welfare of the people by minimising inequalities in income, status, and opportunities.

articles.title: Certain principles of policy to be followed by the State
articles.s: Lays down policy goals: adequate means of livelihood for all, ownership and control of material resources for the common good, no concentration of wealth, equal pay for equal work, protection of workers' health and strength, and protection of children against exploitation.
articles.detail: It lays down principles for both men and women equally, including an adequate means of livelihood, fair distribution of resources, equal pay for equal work, and protection of workers and children from exploitation.

articles.title: Equal justice and free legal aid
articles.s: Directs the State to provide free legal aid so that justice is not denied for economic reasons (42nd Amendment 1976); implemented through the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 and NALSA.
articles.detail: It directs the state to provide free legal aid so that justice is not denied for economic reasons.

articles.title: Organisation of village panchayats
articles.s: Directs the State to organise village panchayats as units of self-government; given constitutional shape by the 73rd Amendment 1992 (Part IX).
articles.detail: It directs the state to organise village panchayats and give them powers to function as units of self-government.

articles.title: Right to work, to education and to public assistance in certain cases
articles.s: Directs the State to secure the right to work, to education and to public assistance in unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, within the limits of its economic capacity.
articles.detail: It directs the state to secure the right to work, to education, and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, and sickness, within its economic capacity.

articles.title: Provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
articles.s: Directs the State to secure just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief for women workers (basis of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961).
articles.detail: It directs the state to secure just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.

articles.title: Living wage, etc., for workers
articles.s: Directs the State to secure a living wage, decent conditions of work and leisure for workers, and to promote cottage industries in rural areas.
articles.detail: It directs the state to secure a living wage and decent conditions of work for all workers.

articles.title: Participation of workers in management of industries
articles.s: Directs the State to secure workers' participation in the management of industrial undertakings (42nd Amendment 1976).

articles.title: Promotion of co-operative societies
articles.s: Directs the State to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies (97th Amendment 2011).

articles.title: Uniform civil code for the citizens
articles.s: Directs the State to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens; discussed in Shah Bano (1985) and ongoing personal-law debates. Uttarakhand enacted a state UCC in 2024.
articles.detail: It directs the state to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens throughout India.

articles.title: Provision for early childhood care and education to children below the age of six years
articles.s: Directs the State to provide early childhood care and education for children below six (as substituted by the 86th Amendment 2002; the earlier free-compulsory-education mandate became the fundamental right in Article 21A).
articles.detail: It directs the state to provide early childhood care and education for all children below six years of age.

articles.title: Promotion of educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections
articles.s: Directs the State to promote the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections with special care, and protect them from social injustice and exploitation.
articles.detail: It directs the state to promote the educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and other weaker sections.

articles.title: Duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living and to improve public health
articles.s: Makes raising nutrition, living standards and public health a primary duty of the State, and directs it to endeavour to prohibit intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health.
articles.detail: It directs the state to raise nutrition levels and improve public health, and to prohibit intoxicating drinks and drugs harmful to health.

articles.title: Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
articles.s: Directs the State to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines and to prohibit the slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle.
articles.detail: It directs the state to organise agriculture and animal husbandry, and to prohibit the slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch and draught cattle.

articles.title: Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life
articles.s: Directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife (42nd Amendment 1976).
articles.detail: It directs the state to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.

articles.title: Protection of monuments and places and objects of national importance
articles.s: Makes it the State's duty to protect every monument, place or object of artistic or historic interest declared of national importance from spoliation, disfigurement and destruction.
articles.detail: It directs the state to protect monuments and places of artistic or historic interest from damage and destruction.

articles.title: Separation of judiciary from executive
articles.s: Directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services (the basis of an independent subordinate judiciary).
articles.detail: It directs the state to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services.

articles.title: Promotion of international peace and security
articles.s: Directs the State to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
articles.detail: It directs the state to promote international peace and security and maintain just relations between nations.

articles.title: Fundamental duties
articles.s: Lists eleven duties of every citizen: respect the Constitution, cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle, protect India's sovereignty and integrity, defend the country, promote harmony and brotherhood, preserve the composite culture, protect the environment, develop scientific temper, safeguard public property, strive for excellence, and provide education to children aged 6 to 14. Ten were added by the 42nd Amendment 1976; the eleventh by the 86th Amendment 2002.
articles.detail: It lists the Fundamental Duties of citizens. These are covered in detail in our Constitution summary for UPSC and law aspirants. This is a study summary for exam preparation; for legal purposes, always consult the official text of the Constitution of India.

articles.title: The President of India
articles.s: There shall be a President of India, the head of state and formal executive head of the Union.
articles.detail: It provides that there shall be a President of India.

articles.title: Executive power of the Union
articles.s: Vests the Union's executive power in the President, exercisable directly or through subordinate officers; the President is also the supreme commander of the defence forces.
articles.detail: It vests the executive power of the Union in the President, to be exercised directly or through officers subordinate to him.

articles.title: Election of President
articles.s: The President is elected by an electoral college of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected MLAs of the states (including Delhi and Puducherry), not by direct popular vote.
articles.detail: It provides for the election of the President by an electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs.

articles.title: Manner of election of President
articles.s: Prescribes proportional representation by single transferable vote with secret ballot; each MLA's vote value is weighted by state population so that all states have uniform weight.
articles.detail: It lays down the manner of the President's election, giving weightage to votes based on population.

articles.title: Term of office of President
articles.s: The President holds office for five years, may resign by writing to the Vice-President, may be removed by impeachment, and continues until a successor takes over.

articles.title: Eligibility for re-election
articles.s: A person who holds or has held the office of President is eligible for re-election; there is no term limit.

articles.title: Qualifications for election as President
articles.s: A candidate must be an Indian citizen, at least 35 years old, qualified for election to the Lok Sabha, and must not hold any office of profit.

articles.title: Conditions of President's office
articles.s: The President cannot be an MP or MLA, cannot hold any other office of profit, and is entitled to fixed emoluments, allowances and privileges during the term.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by the President
articles.s: The President takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law, administered by the Chief Justice of India (or the senior-most SC judge available).

articles.title: Procedure for impeachment of the President
articles.s: Impeachment charges may be preferred by either House with signatures of one-fourth of its members and 14 days' notice, and must be passed by a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House; the President may appear and be represented during investigation.
articles.detail: It lays down the procedure for the impeachment of the President for violation of the Constitution.

articles.title: Time of holding election to fill vacancy in the office of President and the term of office of person elected to fill casual vacancy
articles.s: An election to fill a Presidential vacancy must be held within six months; a person elected to a casual vacancy serves a full five-year term.

articles.title: The Vice-President of India
articles.s: There shall be a Vice-President of India, the second-highest constitutional office in the country.

articles.title: The Vice-President to be ex officio Chairman of the Council of States
articles.s: The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and does not vote except to break a tie as the presiding officer.

articles.title: The Vice-President to act as President or to discharge his functions during casual vacancies in the office, or during the absence, of President
articles.s: The Vice-President acts as President during a vacancy or the President's temporary absence; when acting during a vacancy, a new President must be elected within six months.

articles.title: Election of Vice-President
articles.s: The Vice-President is elected by an electoral college of all members (elected and nominated) of both Houses of Parliament, by proportional representation with single transferable vote.

articles.title: Term of office of Vice-President
articles.s: The Vice-President holds office for five years; may be removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a majority of all its members and agreed to by the Lok Sabha, with at least 14 days' notice.

articles.title: Time of holding election to fill vacancy in the office of Vice-President and the term of office of person elected to fill casual vacancy
articles.s: An election to fill a Vice-Presidential vacancy is held as soon as possible after the vacancy; a person elected to a casual vacancy serves a full five-year term.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by the Vice-President
articles.s: The Vice-President takes the oath of office before the President (or a person appointed by the President).

articles.title: Discharge of President's functions in other contingencies
articles.s: Parliament may provide for discharge of the President's functions in contingencies not covered elsewhere; under the 1969 Act, the CJI (then the senior-most SC judge) discharges the functions.

articles.title: Matters relating to, or connected with, the election of a President or Vice-President
articles.s: Disputes about the election of the President or Vice-President are decided only by the Supreme Court, whose decision is final; Parliament may regulate related matters by law.

articles.title: Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases
articles.s: Gives the President power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions and commutations in court-martial cases, offences against Union laws, and all death sentences; this power is wider than the Governor's under Article 161.
articles.detail: It gives the President the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, and remissions of punishment, including in death sentence cases.

articles.title: Extent of executive power of the Union
articles.s: The Union's executive power extends to matters on which Parliament can legislate and to the exercise of treaty rights, but not into the states' exclusive legislative field except as the Constitution provides.

articles.title: Council of Ministers to aid and advise President
articles.s: There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, who shall act in accordance with that advice; the President may require the Council to reconsider its advice once (position settled by the 42nd and 44th Amendments).
articles.detail: It provides for a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President.

articles.title: Other provisions as to Ministers
articles.s: The Prime Minister is appointed by the President and other ministers on the PM's advice; ministers hold office during the President's pleasure; the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; a minister must become an MP within six months; total ministers cannot exceed 15 percent of Lok Sabha strength (91st Amendment 2003).
articles.detail: It provides that the Prime Minister is appointed by the President, other ministers on the PM's advice, and that the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

articles.title: Attorney-General for India
articles.s: The President appoints the Attorney-General, the Union government's chief legal adviser, who must be qualified to be an SC judge; the AG has the right of audience in all courts and may take part in Parliament without voting.
articles.detail: It provides for the Attorney-General of India, the chief legal adviser to the government, appointed by the President.

articles.title: Conduct of business of the Government of India
articles.s: All executive action of the Government of India is taken in the President's name; the President makes rules for the convenient transaction of business and its allocation among ministers.

articles.title: Duties of Prime Minister as respects the furnishing of information to the President, etc.
articles.s: It is the Prime Minister's duty to communicate Council of Ministers decisions and legislative proposals to the President, furnish information the President calls for, and submit for the Council's consideration any matter decided by a minister alone if the President so requires.

articles.title: Constitution of Parliament
articles.s: Parliament consists of the President, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha).
articles.detail: It provides that Parliament consists of the President, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha), and the House of the People (Lok Sabha).

articles.title: Composition of the Council of States
articles.s: The Rajya Sabha has up to 250 members: 238 representing states and Union Territories (elected by MLAs by proportional representation) and 12 nominated by the President from literature, science, art and social service; it is a permanent body not subject to dissolution.
articles.detail: It deals with the composition of the Rajya Sabha: not more than 250 members, of whom 238 represent states and union territories and 12 are nominated by the President for their contribution to art, literature, science, and social service.

articles.title: Composition of the House of the People
articles.s: The Lok Sabha has up to 552 members (530 from states, 20 from Union Territories, plus 2 formerly nominated Anglo-Indians, now omitted); members are directly elected by the people; its normal term is five years.
articles.detail: It deals with the composition of the Lok Sabha, with a maximum strength of 552 members.

articles.title: Readjustment after each census
articles.s: After every census, Parliament readjusts Lok Sabha seat allocation and constituency delimitation by law; the 84th Amendment froze this on the 1971 census figures until after 2026.

articles.title: Duration of Houses of Parliament
articles.s: The Rajya Sabha is a continuing body with one-third of members retiring every two years; the Lok Sabha's normal duration is five years unless dissolved sooner, extendable by one year at a time during a National Emergency.
articles.detail: It fixes the duration of the Houses of Parliament: the Lok Sabha normally lasts five years, while the Rajya Sabha is a continuing body with one-third of members retiring every two years.

articles.title: Qualification for membership of Parliament
articles.s: To be an MP a person must be an Indian citizen, at least 30 years old for the Rajya Sabha and 25 for the Lok Sabha, and possess other qualifications prescribed by Parliament (Representation of the People Act, 1951).

articles.title: Sessions of Parliament, prorogation and dissolution
articles.s: The President summons each House (the gap between two sessions cannot exceed six months), may prorogue the Houses, and may dissolve the Lok Sabha.
articles.detail: It gives the President the power to summon and prorogue Parliament and to dissolve the Lok Sabha.

articles.title: Right of President to address and send messages to Houses
articles.s: The President may address either House of Parliament or both Houses together, and may send messages on Bills pending in Parliament.

articles.title: Special address by the President
articles.s: The President addresses both Houses assembled together at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year, laying out the government's policy agenda.

articles.title: Rights of Ministers and Attorney-General as respects Houses
articles.s: Every minister and the Attorney-General may speak and take part in the proceedings of either House and its committees, but may vote only in the House of which they are members.

articles.title: The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States
articles.s: The Vice-President is the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; the House elects a Deputy Chairman from among its members.

articles.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the office of Deputy Chairman
articles.s: The Deputy Chairman vacates office on ceasing to be a Rajya Sabha member, by resigning to the Chairman, or by removal through a resolution passed by a majority of all members of the House.

articles.title: Power of the Deputy Chairman or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Chairman
articles.s: The Deputy Chairman (or a member fixed by the rules, or a person appointed by the President) performs the Chairman's duties during a vacancy or absence.

articles.title: The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
articles.s: The Chairman or Deputy Chairman must vacate the chair while a resolution for their removal is under consideration, though they may be present; the Chairman may vote only to break a tie.

articles.title: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People
articles.s: The Lok Sabha chooses two of its members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker, as soon as possible after it is constituted.

articles.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker
articles.s: The Speaker or Deputy Speaker vacates office on ceasing to be an MP, by resignation, or by removal through a Lok Sabha resolution passed by a majority of all members with at least 14 days' notice.

articles.title: Power of the Deputy Speaker or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Speaker
articles.s: The Deputy Speaker (or a member fixed by the rules, or a person chosen by the House) performs the Speaker's duties during a vacancy or absence.

articles.title: The Speaker or the Deputy Speaker not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
articles.s: The Speaker or Deputy Speaker must vacate the chair while their own removal resolution is considered, but unlike the Rajya Sabha Chairman they may vote in the first instance.

articles.title: Salaries and allowances of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker
articles.s: Their salaries and allowances are fixed by Parliament by law and charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

articles.title: Secretariat of Parliament
articles.s: Each House of Parliament has its own separate secretariat, with Parliament regulating their recruitment and service conditions by law.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by members
articles.s: Every MP must take an oath or affirmation in the Third Schedule form before taking a seat in Parliament.

articles.title: Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum
articles.s: Decisions are taken by a majority of members present and voting (the presiding officer votes only on a tie); a House may act despite vacancies; quorum is one-tenth of the House's total membership.

articles.title: Vacation of seats
articles.s: An MP's seat falls vacant on disqualification under Article 102, on resignation, on 60 days' absence without permission, or on holding both Houses' seats; the House may declare the seat vacant.

articles.title: Disqualifications for membership
articles.s: Disqualified if the person holds an office of profit, is of unsound mind, is an undischarged insolvent, is not an Indian citizen or has voluntarily acquired foreign citizenship, or is disqualified under any Parliamentary law (such as the Tenth Schedule).

articles.title: Decision on questions as to disqualifications of members
articles.s: The President decides disqualification questions under Article 102, in accordance with the Election Commission's opinion.

articles.title: Penalty for sitting and voting before making oath or affirmation under article 99 or when not qualified or when disqualified
articles.s: An unqualified person who sits or votes in Parliament is liable to a fine of five hundred rupees for each day.

articles.title: Powers, privileges, etc., of the Houses of Parliament and of the members and committees thereof
articles.s: MPs enjoy freedom of speech in Parliament, immunity from court proceedings for votes and speeches, and the House's powers and privileges as defined by Parliament (key cases: Keshav Singh, JMM bribery case).

articles.title: Salaries and allowances of members
articles.s: MPs' salaries and allowances are fixed by Parliament by law.

articles.title: Provisions as to introduction and passing of Bills
articles.s: A Bill may originate in either House (except Money Bills); it must be passed by both Houses and receive the President's assent to become law; a Bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on dissolution.

articles.title: Joint sitting of both Houses in certain cases
articles.s: If the Houses disagree on a Bill, the President may summon a joint sitting (except for Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills); the decision is by a majority of those present and voting (used in 1961, 1978 and 2002).
articles.detail: It provides for a joint sitting of both Houses, presided over by the Speaker, to resolve deadlocks on ordinary bills. It does not apply to money bills or constitutional amendment bills.

articles.title: Special procedure in respect of Money Bills
articles.s: Money Bills may be introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation; the Rajya Sabha has 14 days to recommend amendments, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject.

articles.title: Definition of "Money Bills"
articles.s: A Bill is a Money Bill only if it deals exclusively with taxation, borrowing, the Consolidated or Contingency Funds, appropriation, or audit and accounts (the Aadhaar Act's Money Bill certification was litigated in Rojer Mathew).
articles.detail: It defines a money bill and declares that the Speaker's decision on whether a bill is a money bill is final.

articles.title: Assent to Bills
articles.s: The President may assent to a Bill, withhold assent, or return a non-Money Bill for reconsideration; on reconsideration and re-passing, the President must assent (used for the office-of-profit Bill in 2006).

articles.title: Annual financial statement
articles.s: The President causes the Annual Financial Statement (the Union Budget) to be laid before Parliament each year, showing estimated receipts and expenditure.
articles.detail: It requires the President to lay the Annual Financial Statement, commonly called the Union Budget, before Parliament every year.

articles.title: Procedure in Parliament with respect to estimates
articles.s: Estimates are presented as demands for grants voted by the Lok Sabha; no demand can be made without the President's recommendation.

articles.title: Appropriation Bills
articles.s: After grants are voted, an Appropriation Bill authorises withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund of India to meet those grants; no amendment varying the amount is allowed.

articles.title: Supplementary, additional or excess grants
articles.s: The President may lay before Parliament supplementary, additional or excess demands when authorised expenditure proves insufficient or money is spent beyond the grant.

articles.title: Votes on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants
articles.s: The Lok Sabha may grant a vote on account in advance pending the budget, votes of credit for indefinite demands, and exceptional grants outside the normal service of the year.

articles.title: Special provisions as to financial Bills
articles.s: Financial Bills of category I and II follow special procedures; Bills like Money Bills need the President's prior recommendation and cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha.

articles.title: Rules of procedure
articles.s: Each House of Parliament makes its own rules of procedure and conduct of business.

articles.title: Regulation by law of procedure in Parliament in relation to financial business
articles.s: Parliament may by law regulate its financial-business procedure to ensure timely completion of financial business.

articles.title: Language to be used in Parliament
articles.s: Business is transacted in Hindi or English; after 15 years from commencement, English could be dropped unless Parliament provided otherwise, and Parliament has continued it (Official Languages Act, 1963).

articles.title: Restriction on discussion in Parliament
articles.s: No discussion may take place in Parliament about the conduct of any Supreme Court or High Court judge in the discharge of duties, except on a motion for removal (Article 124(4)).

articles.title: Courts not to inquire into proceedings of Parliament
articles.s: Courts cannot question the validity of Parliamentary proceedings for alleged irregularity of procedure (this protects internal proceedings, not illegal unconstitutional acts).

articles.title: Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament
articles.s: The President may promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session if immediate action is needed; an ordinance has the force of law but must be laid before Parliament and lapses six weeks after reassembly (R.C. Cooper; ordinances cannot be a parallel legislative tool).
articles.detail: It gives the President the power to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session. An ordinance has the force of law but lapses if not approved within six weeks of Parliament reassembling.

articles.title: Establishment and constitution of Supreme Court
articles.s: Establishes the Supreme Court of India with a Chief Justice and up to 33 other judges (originally 7, raised by the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act); judges are appointed by the President under the collegium system (NJAC Act struck down in 2015).
articles.detail: It provides for the establishment of the Supreme Court of India.

articles.title: Salaries, etc., of Judges
articles.s: Supreme Court judges' salaries and allowances are fixed by Parliament by law and charged on the Consolidated Fund of India; they cannot be varied to a judge's disadvantage.

articles.title: Appointment of acting Chief Justice
articles.s: When the Chief Justice's office is vacant or the CJI is absent or unable to perform duties, the President appoints another SC judge as acting Chief Justice.

articles.title: Appointment of ad hoc judges
articles.s: The Chief Justice, with the President's prior consent, may request a High Court judge qualified for the SC to sit as an ad hoc judge when the Court lacks quorum.

articles.title: Attendance of retired Judges at sittings of the Supreme Court
articles.s: The Chief Justice, with the President's prior consent, may request a retired SC or High Court judge to sit and act as a judge of the Supreme Court.

articles.title: Supreme Court to be a court of record
articles.s: The Supreme Court is a court of record with the power to punish for its own contempt (Contempt of Courts Act, 1971).
articles.detail: It declares the Supreme Court a court of record, meaning its judgments are recorded and have evidentiary value.

articles.title: Seat of Supreme Court
articles.s: The Supreme Court sits in Delhi; the Chief Justice, with the President's approval, may appoint other places for sittings.

articles.title: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
articles.s: The Supreme Court has exclusive original jurisdiction over disputes between the Union and states or between states (used in inter-state disputes like the Cauvery matter).

articles.title: Exclusive jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in regard to questions as to constitutional validity of Central laws
articles.s: Inserted by the 42nd Amendment 1976 giving the SC exclusive jurisdiction over the constitutional validity of central laws; omitted by the 43rd Amendment 1977.

articles.title: Appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court in appeals from High Courts in certain cases
articles.s: An appeal lies to the Supreme Court from a High Court judgment involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, on the High Court's certificate.

articles.title: Appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court in appeals from High Courts in regard to civil matters
articles.s: An appeal lies in civil matters on the High Court's certificate that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance needing the Supreme Court's decision.

articles.title: Appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court in regard to criminal matters
articles.s: An appeal lies in criminal matters where the High Court reversed an acquittal and sentenced to death, withdrew a case to itself and sentenced to death, or certifies the case fit for appeal.

articles.title: Certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court
articles.s: Every High Court passing or making a judgment, decree, final order or sentence must consider whether to grant a certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court (42nd Amendment 1976).

articles.title: Jurisdiction and powers of the Federal Court under existing law to be exercisable by the Supreme Court
articles.s: The Supreme Court exercises the jurisdiction and powers of the former Federal Court under pre-Constitution laws until Parliament provides otherwise.

articles.title: Special leave to appeal by the Supreme Court
articles.s: The Supreme Court may in its discretion grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree or order of any court or tribunal in India (not applying to armed forces tribunals).
articles.detail: It gives the Supreme Court discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal against any judgment of any court or tribunal in India.

articles.title: Review of judgments or orders by the Supreme Court
articles.s: The Supreme Court may review its own judgments or orders, subject to Parliamentary law and its own rules (review petitions, and curative petitions after Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002).

articles.title: Enlargement of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
articles.s: Parliament may by law enlarge the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and powers with respect to matters in the Union List, and by special agreement for other matters.

articles.title: Conferment on the Supreme Court of powers to issue certain writs
articles.s: Parliament may confer on the Supreme Court power to issue writs (other than for Fundamental Rights, covered by Article 32) for any other purpose.

articles.title: Transfer of certain cases
articles.s: The Supreme Court may transfer cases involving the same or substantially the same question of law pending before it and one or more High Courts to itself, or transfer cases between High Courts (42nd Amendment 1976).

articles.title: Ancillary powers of Supreme Court
articles.s: Parliament may confer supplementary powers on the Supreme Court to make its jurisdiction effective.

articles.title: Law declared by Supreme Court to be binding on all courts
articles.s: The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India (the doctrine of precedent; Article 141 underpins stare decisis).
articles.detail: It declares that the law laid down by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India.

articles.title: Enforcement of decrees and orders of Supreme Court and orders as to discovery, etc.
articles.s: The Supreme Court may pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in a case (Article 142's 'complete justice' power), enforceable throughout India.
articles.detail: It empowers the Supreme Court to pass any order necessary for doing complete justice in a case before it.

articles.title: Power of President to consult Supreme Court
articles.s: The President may refer questions of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion, which is not binding (used in the Ayodhya reference and the 2G reference).
articles.detail: It gives the President the power to seek the Supreme Court's advisory opinion on questions of law or public importance.

articles.title: Civil and judicial authorities to act in aid of the Supreme Court
articles.s: All civil and judicial authorities in India must act in aid of the Supreme Court.
articles.detail: It requires all civil and judicial authorities in India to act in aid of the Supreme Court.

articles.title: Rules of Court, etc.
articles.s: The Supreme Court makes rules regulating its practice and procedure, subject to Parliamentary law and the President's approval.

articles.title: Officers and servants and the expenses of the Supreme Court
articles.s: The Chief Justice appoints the Court's officers and servants; administrative expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

articles.title: Interpretation
articles.s: Defines 'a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution' and related expressions used in this Chapter.

articles.title: Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
articles.s: There shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India appointed by the President, removable only like an SC judge, who audits the accounts of the Union and the states.

articles.title: Duties and powers of the Comptroller and Auditor-General
articles.s: The CAG performs duties and exercises powers prescribed by Parliament (CAG's (DPC) Act, 1971), covering Union, state and public-sector accounts.

articles.title: Form of accounts of the Union and of the States
articles.s: The Union and state accounts are kept in the form prescribed by the President on the CAG's advice.

articles.title: Audit reports
articles.s: The CAG's reports on Union accounts go to the President, who lays them before Parliament; state reports go to the Governor for the state legislature.

articles.title: Definition
articles.s: For this Part, 'State' does not include Jammu and Kashmir as originally framed; after the 2019 reorganisation the definition's application changed accordingly.

articles.title: Governors of States
articles.s: There shall be a Governor for each state; one person may be appointed Governor of two or more states.

articles.title: Executive power of State
articles.s: Vests the state's executive power in the Governor, exercisable directly or through subordinate officers.

articles.title: Appointment of Governor
articles.s: The Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.

articles.title: Term of office of Governor
articles.s: The Governor holds office for five years but serves during the President's pleasure, may resign to the President, and continues until a successor takes over.

articles.title: Qualifications for appointment as Governor
articles.s: A person must be an Indian citizen and at least 35 years old to be appointed Governor.

articles.title: Conditions of Governor's office
articles.s: The Governor cannot be an MP or MLA, cannot hold any other office of profit, and is entitled to fixed emoluments, allowances and privileges.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by the Governor
articles.s: The Governor takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution, administered by the Chief Justice of the High Court (or the senior-most judge available).

articles.title: Discharge of the functions of the Governor in certain contingencies
articles.s: The President may make provisions for discharge of the Governor's functions in contingencies not provided for in this Chapter.

articles.title: Power of Governor to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases
articles.s: The Governor may grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions and commutations in state-law offences, but has no power over death sentences (unlike the President under Article 72).

articles.title: Extent of executive power of State
articles.s: The state's executive power extends to matters on which the state legislature can legislate.

articles.title: Council of Ministers to aid and advise Governor
articles.s: There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Chief Minister at the head to aid and advise the Governor, who acts on that advice except where the Constitution requires discretion (position clarified by the 42nd and 44th Amendments and the S.R. Bommai case).

articles.title: Other provisions as to Ministers
articles.s: The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor and other ministers on the CM's advice; ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure; the Council is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly; total ministers cannot exceed 15 percent of the Assembly strength with a minimum of 12 (91st Amendment 2003).

articles.title: Advocate-General for the State
articles.s: The Governor appoints the Advocate-General, the state's chief legal adviser, who must be qualified to be a High Court judge and has the right of audience in all courts in the state.

articles.title: Conduct of business of the Government of a State
articles.s: All executive action of a state government is taken in the Governor's name; the Governor makes rules for the transaction of business and its allocation among ministers.

articles.title: Duties of Chief Minister as respects the furnishing of information to Governor, etc.
articles.s: The Chief Minister must communicate Council of Ministers decisions and legislative proposals to the Governor, furnish information the Governor calls for, and submit for the Council's consideration any matter decided by a minister alone if the Governor so requires.

articles.title: Constitution of Legislatures in States
articles.s: Every state has a legislature of the Governor plus either two Houses (Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council) or one House; six states currently have Councils: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh.

articles.title: Abolition or creation of Legislative Councils in States
articles.s: Parliament may by law abolish or create a Legislative Council in a state if the state's Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority; such laws need only a simple majority in Parliament.

articles.title: Composition of the Legislative Assemblies
articles.s: An Assembly has between 60 and 500 members directly elected from territorial constituencies; each state is divided into constituencies so that the population-to-seat ratio is broadly uniform.

articles.title: Composition of the Legislative Councils
articles.s: A Legislative Council has up to one-third of the Assembly's strength (minimum 40); members are elected by local bodies, graduates, teachers and MLAs, with the rest nominated by the Governor from distinguished fields.

articles.title: Duration of State Legislatures
articles.s: An Assembly's normal duration is five years unless dissolved sooner, extendable by one year at a time during a National Emergency; the Council is a continuing body with one-third retiring every two years.

articles.title: Qualification for membership of the State Legislature
articles.s: To be an MLA or MLC a person must be an Indian citizen, at least 25 years old for the Assembly and 30 for the Council, and possess other qualifications prescribed by Parliament.

articles.title: Sessions of the State Legislature, prorogation and dissolution
articles.s: The Governor summons each House (the gap between two sessions cannot exceed six months), may prorogue the Houses, and may dissolve the Assembly.

articles.title: Right of Governor to address and send messages to the House or Houses
articles.s: The Governor may address the legislature and send messages on Bills, which the House must consider.

articles.title: Special address by the Governor
articles.s: The Governor addresses the legislature at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year.

articles.title: Rights of Ministers and Advocate-General as respects the Houses
articles.s: Every minister and the Advocate-General may speak and take part in either House's proceedings and committees, but may vote only in the House of which they are members.

articles.title: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
articles.s: The Assembly chooses two of its members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker.

articles.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker
articles.s: The Speaker or Deputy Speaker vacates office on ceasing to be an MLA, by resignation, or by removal through an Assembly resolution passed by a majority of all members with at least 14 days' notice.

articles.title: Power of the Deputy Speaker or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Speaker
articles.s: The Deputy Speaker (or a member fixed by the rules) performs the Speaker's duties during a vacancy or absence.

articles.title: The Speaker or the Deputy Speaker not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
articles.s: The Speaker or Deputy Speaker must vacate the chair while their own removal resolution is considered, but may vote in the first instance.

articles.title: The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council
articles.s: The Council chooses a Chairman and Deputy Chairman from among its members.

articles.title: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Chairman and Deputy Chairman
articles.s: The Chairman or Deputy Chairman vacates office on ceasing to be an MLC, by resignation, or by removal through a Council resolution passed by a majority of all members.

articles.title: Power of the Deputy Chairman or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Chairman
articles.s: The Deputy Chairman (or a member fixed by the rules) performs the Chairman's duties during a vacancy or absence.

articles.title: The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
articles.s: The Chairman or Deputy Chairman must vacate the chair while their own removal resolution is considered, though they may be present.

articles.title: Salaries and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman
articles.s: Their salaries and allowances are fixed by the state legislature by law and charged on the state's Consolidated Fund.

articles.title: Secretariat of State Legislature
articles.s: Each House of a state legislature has its own separate secretariat, with the legislature regulating recruitment and service conditions by law.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by members
articles.s: Every MLA or MLC must take an oath or affirmation in the Third Schedule form before taking a seat.

articles.title: Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum
articles.s: Decisions are by a majority of members present and voting (the presiding officer votes only on a tie); a House may act despite vacancies; quorum is ten members or one-tenth of the House, whichever is greater.

articles.title: Vacation of seats
articles.s: An MLA's or MLC's seat falls vacant on disqualification under Article 191, on resignation, on 60 days' absence without permission, or on holding seats in both Houses; the House may declare the seat vacant.

articles.title: Disqualifications for membership
articles.s: Disqualified if the person holds an office of profit, is of unsound mind, is an undischarged insolvent, is not an Indian citizen or has acquired foreign citizenship, or is disqualified under any Parliamentary law (such as the Tenth Schedule).

articles.title: Decision on questions as to disqualifications of members
articles.s: The Governor decides disqualification questions under Article 191, in accordance with the Election Commission's opinion.

articles.title: Penalty for sitting and voting before making oath or affirmation under article 188 or when not qualified or when disqualified
articles.s: An unqualified person who sits or votes in the legislature is liable to a fine of five hundred rupees for each day.

articles.title: Powers, privileges, etc., of the Houses of Legislatures and of the members and committees thereof
articles.s: MLAs and MLCs enjoy freedom of speech in the legislature, immunity from court proceedings for votes and speeches, and the House's powers and privileges as defined by the legislature.

articles.title: Salaries and allowances of members
articles.s: MLAs' and MLCs' salaries and allowances are fixed by the state legislature by law.

articles.title: Provisions as to introduction and passing of Bills
articles.s: A Bill may originate in either House (except Money Bills); it must be passed by the legislature and receive the Governor's assent to become law.

articles.title: Restriction on powers of Legislative Council as to Bills other than Money Bills
articles.s: The Council may only delay an ordinary Bill: if the Assembly passes it a second time after three months (one month in the second passage), it is deemed passed by the Council (the Council has at most about four months' delaying power).

articles.title: Special procedure in respect of Money Bills
articles.s: Money Bills may be introduced only in the Assembly on the Governor's recommendation; the Council has 14 days to recommend amendments, which the Assembly may accept or reject.

articles.title: Definition of "Money Bills"
articles.s: A Bill is a Money Bill only if it deals exclusively with taxation, borrowing, the Consolidated or Contingency Funds, appropriation, or audit and accounts; the Speaker's certificate is final.

articles.title: Assent to Bills
articles.s: The Governor may assent to a Bill, withhold assent, reserve it for the President's consideration, or return a non-Money Bill for reconsideration; on re-passing, the Governor must assent (the Governor's discretion here is much litigated, e.g. in recent Tamil Nadu and Punjab disputes).

articles.title: Bills reserved for consideration
articles.s: When a Bill is reserved for the President, the President may assent, withhold assent, or direct the Governor to return it for reconsideration within six months; the President is not bound to assent even on re-passing.

articles.title: Annual financial statement
articles.s: The Governor causes the Annual Financial Statement (the state budget) to be laid before the legislature each year.

articles.title: Procedure in Legislature with respect to estimates
articles.s: Estimates are presented as demands for grants voted by the Assembly; no demand can be made without the Governor's recommendation.

articles.title: Appropriation Bills
articles.s: After grants are voted, an Appropriation Bill authorises withdrawal from the state's Consolidated Fund; no amendment varying the amount is allowed.

articles.title: Supplementary, additional or excess grants
articles.s: The Governor may lay supplementary, additional or excess demands before the legislature when authorised expenditure proves insufficient.

articles.title: Votes on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants
articles.s: The Assembly may grant a vote on account in advance pending the budget, votes of credit for indefinite demands, and exceptional grants.

articles.title: Special provisions as to financial Bills
articles.s: Financial Bills need the Governor's prior recommendation and cannot be introduced in the Legislative Council.

articles.title: Rules of procedure
articles.s: Each House of the legislature makes its own rules of procedure and conduct of business.

articles.title: Regulation by law of procedure in the Legislature of the State in relation to financial business
articles.s: The state legislature may by law regulate its financial-business procedure to ensure timely completion.

articles.title: Language to be used in the Legislature
articles.s: Business is transacted in the state's official language, Hindi or English; English use could be discontinued after 15 years unless continued by the legislature.

articles.title: Restriction on discussion in the Legislature
articles.s: No discussion may take place about the conduct of any Supreme Court or High Court judge except on a motion for removal.

articles.title: Courts not to inquire into proceedings of the Legislature
articles.s: Courts cannot question the validity of legislative proceedings for alleged irregularity of procedure.

articles.title: Power of Governor to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Legislature
articles.s: The Governor may promulgate ordinances when the legislature is not in session if immediate action is needed; an ordinance must be laid before the legislature and lapses six weeks after reassembly.

articles.title: High Courts for States
articles.s: There shall be a High Court for each state (one High Court may serve two or more states, such as the common High Court for Punjab and Haryana).
articles.detail: It provides for a High Court for each state.

articles.title: High Courts to be courts of record
articles.s: Every High Court is a court of record with the power to punish for its own contempt.

articles.title: Constitution of High Courts
articles.s: Each High Court consists of a Chief Justice and other judges as the President appoints; judges are appointed by the President under the collegium system.

articles.title: Appointment and conditions of the office of a Judge of a High Court
articles.s: High Court judges are appointed by the President; they hold office until age 62 and may be removed only like SC judges (Articles 124(4) and (5)).

articles.title: Application of certain provisions relating to Supreme Court to High Courts
articles.s: The provisions on judges' salaries, oath and removal (Articles 124(4) and (5)) apply to High Court judges as well.

articles.title: Oath or affirmation by Judges of High Courts
articles.s: A High Court judge takes the oath in the Third Schedule form before the Governor (or a person appointed by the Governor).

articles.title: Restriction on practice after being a permanent Judge
articles.s: A permanent High Court judge cannot plead or act in any court or before any authority in India except the Supreme Court and other High Courts.

articles.title: Salaries, etc., of Judges
articles.s: High Court judges' salaries and allowances are fixed by Parliament by law and charged on the state's Consolidated Fund; they cannot be varied to a judge's disadvantage.

articles.title: Transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another
articles.s: The President may, after consulting the Chief Justice of India, transfer a High Court judge to another High Court (judicial review of transfers was recognised in the First Judges case).

articles.title: Appointment of acting Chief Justice
articles.s: When the Chief Justice's office is vacant or the CJ is absent or unable to perform duties, the President appoints another judge as acting Chief Justice.

articles.title: Appointment of additional and acting Judges
articles.s: The President may appoint additional judges for temporary workload increases (up to two years) and acting judges during a permanent judge's absence.

articles.title: Appointment of retired Judges at sittings of High Courts
articles.s: The Chief Justice of a High Court, with the President's prior consent, may request a retired High Court judge to sit and act as a judge (42nd Amendment 1976).

articles.title: Jurisdiction of existing High Courts
articles.s: The existing High Courts' jurisdiction and the laws on their powers continue, subject to the Constitution and laws made by the appropriate legislature.

articles.title: Power of High Courts to issue certain writs
articles.s: Every High Court may issue writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari) for enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose; wider than the Supreme Court's Article 32 power.
articles.detail: It gives High Courts the power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose, making their writ jurisdiction wider than the Supreme Court's under Article 32.

articles.title: Power of superintendence over all courts by the High Court
articles.s: Every High Court has superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory (except military tribunals), including calling for returns and making rules of practice.

articles.title: Transfer of certain cases to High Court
articles.s: A High Court may withdraw to itself a case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution pending in a subordinate court.

articles.title: Officers and servants and the expenses of High Courts
articles.s: The Chief Justice appoints the High Court's officers and servants; administrative expenses are charged on the state's Consolidated Fund.

articles.title: Extension of jurisdiction of High Courts to Union territories
articles.s: Parliament may by law extend or exclude a High Court's jurisdiction to or from a Union Territory.

articles.title: Establishment of a common High Court for two or more States
articles.s: Parliament may by law establish a common High Court for two or more states or for states and a Union Territory (e.g. the former common High Court for the north-eastern states).

articles.title: Interpretation
articles.s: Was an interpretation clause for this Chapter; omitted by the 7th Amendment 1956 when the Part B states were reorganised.

articles.title: Appointment of district judges
articles.s: District judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court; a person not already in judicial service must have seven years' Bar practice and be recommended by the High Court.

articles.title: Validation of appointments of, and judgments, etc., delivered by, certain district judges
articles.s: Validates certain district judge appointments, postings and judgments made before the 20th Amendment 1966 that would otherwise be invalid for procedural defects.

articles.title: Recruitment of persons other than district judges to the judicial service
articles.s: Judicial service appointments below district judge are made by the Governor under rules framed after consulting the State Public Service Commission and the High Court.

articles.title: Control over subordinate courts
articles.s: Control over district and subordinate courts, including postings, promotions and leave, vests in the High Court.

articles.title: Interpretation
articles.s: Defines 'district judge' and 'judicial service' for this Chapter.

articles.title: Application of the provisions of this Chapter to certain class or classes of magistrates
articles.s: The Governor may by public notification apply the subordinate-courts provisions to any class of magistrates in the state, as if references to district judges included those magistrates.

articles.title: Application of provisions of Part VI to States in Part B of the First Schedule
articles.s: Applied Part VI to the former Part B states; became redundant and was omitted by the 7th Amendment 1956.

articles.title: Administration of Union territories
articles.s: Union Territories are administered by the President acting through an Administrator (Lieutenant Governor); the President may also appoint a state's Governor as a UT's Administrator.

articles.title: Special provisions with respect to Delhi
articles.s: Gives the National Capital Territory of Delhi a Legislative Assembly and Council of Ministers with power over State and Concurrent List subjects except public order, police and land; inserted by the 69th Amendment 1991 and interpreted in the 2018 and 2023 Constitution Bench rulings on the LG's powers.

articles.title: Provision in case of failure of constitutional machinery
articles.s: If Delhi's administration cannot be carried on per Article 239AA, the President may suspend provisions of Article 239AA on the Administrator's report (69th Amendment 1991).

articles.title: Power of administrator to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Legislature
articles.s: A UT Administrator may promulgate ordinances when the UT legislature is not in session, with the President's prior instructions; an ordinance lapses six weeks after the legislature reassembles.

articles.title: Power of Parliament to make laws for certain Union territories
articles.s: Parliament may make laws for Union Territories without legislatures on any subject, and the President may make regulations for certain UTs (Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Puducherry in some cases) having the force of Parliamentary Acts.

articles.title: High Courts for Union territories
articles.s: Parliament may by law constitute a High Court for a Union Territory or extend an existing High Court's jurisdiction to it.

articles.title: Coorg
articles.s: Dealt with the Part C state of Coorg; repealed by the 7th Amendment 1956 when Coorg merged into Mysore state.

articles.title: Definitions
articles.s: Defines 'district', 'Gram Sabha', 'intermediate level', 'Panchayat', 'Panchayat area' and 'village' for this Part (73rd Amendment 1992).

articles.title: Gram Sabha
articles.s: A Gram Sabha (all voters of a village) may exercise powers and perform functions at village level as the state legislature provides by law.

articles.title: Constitution of Panchayats
articles.s: There shall be Panchayats at village, intermediate and district levels in every state (intermediate level may be skipped in states below 20 lakh population).
articles.detail: It provides for the constitution of panchayats at the village, intermediate, and district levels.

articles.title: Composition of Panchayats
articles.s: All Panchayat seats are filled by direct election; the chairperson at intermediate and district levels is elected indirectly; MLAs and MPs may be represented as the state legislature provides.

articles.title: Reservation of seats
articles.s: Seats are reserved for SCs and STs in proportion to population, with at least one-third reserved for women (including within SC/ST quotas); states may also reserve seats for backward classes.
articles.detail: It reserves seats in panchayats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and one-third of seats for women.

articles.title: Duration of Panchayats, etc.
articles.s: A Panchayat's term is five years; elections must be completed before its term expires; a dissolved Panchayat's fresh election must be held within six months, and the new body serves only the remainder of the term.

articles.title: Disqualifications for membership
articles.s: A person is disqualified from Panchayat membership if disqualified under any law for the state legislature's election, or under any state law; minimum age 21.

articles.title: Powers, authority and responsibilities of Panchayats
articles.s: State legislatures may endow Panchayats with powers to function as institutions of self-government, including preparing plans for economic development and social justice and implementing schemes in the Eleventh Schedule's 29 subjects.

articles.title: Powers to impose taxes by, and Funds of, the Panchayats
articles.s: State legislatures may authorise Panchayats to levy and collect taxes, assign state revenues to them, and provide for grants-in-aid and Panchayat Funds.

articles.title: Constitution of Finance Commission to review financial position
articles.s: The Governor constitutes a State Finance Commission every five years to review Panchayats' finances and recommend principles for distributing state revenues to them.

articles.title: Audit of accounts of Panchayats
articles.s: State legislatures may provide for maintenance and audit of Panchayat accounts.

articles.title: Elections to the Panchayats
articles.s: Panchayat elections are conducted under the superintendence, direction and control of the State Election Commission.
articles.detail: It provides for a State Election Commission to supervise the elections to panchayats.
